Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' These items describe opposing levels of verbal access to the trauma memory and are hard to reconcile as the same patient's current self-report.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked memory disturbance items ('some moments are extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'there are parts of the event I simply cannot remember'). Although fragmented trauma memory can coexist with disclosure, the wording 'very easily' is hard to reconcile with this level of fragmentation in the same profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
issues.explanation: Across Memory and Negative Appraisals, reporting that one can talk about the event 'very easily' sits in tension with the appraisal 'If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it.' Patients may force themselves to discuss trauma despite distress, but these two statements point in opposite directions and are difficult to integrate clinically without additional context.

vignette:
Tane, a 63-year-old divorced Pacific Islander man, came to treatment after months of trying to carry on with work and family life as if nothing had changed. He had built his life around community organizing in a city neighborhood where he was known for speaking at meetings, mediating disputes, and helping older residents navigate housing and benefits. Before the accident, he was the kind of man who stood at the front of a room with an easy, even voice. Afterward, he found himself avoiding rooms entirely when he could, especially if the discussion might turn heated. In the weeks before seeking help, he was increasingly uneasy in the very spaces that once gave his work meaning: tenant meetings, church gatherings, and office consultations where raised voices or even a calm, controlled tone of anger from another person could make his chest tighten and his attention lock onto the speaker's face, waiting for the moment things might turn.

The traumatic event had occurred years earlier, when Tane was caught in a life-threatening accident that unfolded fast and left him with only fragments he could still hold onto. He could picture some moments with painful clarity: a sudden rush of noise, a sense that everything had gone wrong at once, and the stark sight of uniforms in the middle of the chaos, which remained vivid enough that even now a police officer's presence or a military-style uniform could make his stomach drop. Other parts of that day were blank. He knew the event happened, knew he had been in danger, but there were stretches he could not account for no matter how hard he tried to remember them. When he attempted to tell the story, he often stalled, his face tightening with frustration, because he knew what happened but could not find words that seemed sufficient to describe it. In sessions he would circle a detail, then stop and say that the language was not there, or that the memory broke apart when he tried to explain it in order.

After the accident, Tane noticed that his body seemed to stay on guard long after the danger had passed. He described it not as nerves, but as his body "acting like it never got the message." Even sitting at his kitchen table or walking into a familiar storefront, he would feel keyed up, shoulders tense, heart racing, as if he were still bracing for impact or being watched. This frightened him because it felt involuntary and humiliating, as though his own body had become an unreliable witness. He had come to believe that the event happened because of the way he acted, replaying his choices and wondering whether a different response could have changed everything. He did not describe this as simple regret; it carried the weight of conviction. He would speak about the accident with a kind of blunt self-accusation, as if he should have known better, should have moved faster, should have done something other than what he did in those critical moments he could partially remember.

Alongside this, Tane spoke of feeling dead inside. He used those exact words, saying that since the accident there were stretches of the day when he could function, but without any real sense of warmth or contact. He could do the work, answer the calls, attend to the practical demands of his role, yet he felt emotionally absent from his own life. This numbness had become especially noticeable in his relationships since his divorce, and in the smaller social routines that once gave him a sense of belonging. He was not withdrawn from a single person so much as disconnected from himself, going through the motions while feeling as though some essential part of his emotional life had gone quiet.

His avoidance had formed gradually around these experiences. He started taking different routes to avoid seeing uniformed officers outside courthouses or along the streets near city offices. At work, he became careful about which meetings he attended, often sending notes instead of going in person if he expected tension. When a colleague spoke sharply, even without malice, he felt a surge of alarm and the urge to leave the room. Over time, this narrowed his involvement in the community he had once been central to, and he noticed that others had begun relying on him less because he was harder to reach in person. That change stung, but he also felt unable to push himself back into the same spaces with the same ease.

By the time he sought help, Tane was worried less about whether the accident had happened than about how much of himself was still living in its aftermath. He wanted to be able to sit through a meeting without scanning every face for anger, to see a uniform without feeling his body tense in advance, and to speak about what happened without running out of words or hitting blank spaces he could not cross. What brought him in now was the fear that he was losing more of his life to silence and vigilance, and his hope was simple but urgent: to feel safe enough in his own body and in his own work to stay present again.
